title: The Plan Gets Worse
tagline: Start with one tiny target. End with a blueprint that needs its own blueprint.
premise: You are building one heist plan, one move at a time, while the host hypes every terrible upgrade. Start with a small, harmless target; each player adds the next needed part, and the plan grows louder, stranger, and harder to hide.

seed_pool.opening_token: A tiny museum has one gold coin in a glass box, and the first plan is to get inside during the afternoon tour.
A quiet hotel keeps one famous diamond in a locked display, and the first plan is to enter as guests at breakfast.
A small fairground has one prize watch in the office, and the first plan is to reach it while the rides are running.

tests: It names a small, harmless target and a place a stranger can picture. Present tense, one sentence, plain words.
A player can name one necessary planning step within five seconds, and there is more than one good answer. Say two.
The first plan is only an entry or access idea, not the whole heist. No escape, alarm, getaway, or stolen object is already handled.
Nobody is hurt on the card, no real people, no brands, and no detailed instructions for real crime.
It makes a player want to add one useful part while still leaving room for the plan to become absurd. Never write a full operation as if it were a checklist.

move_constraints.example: Then we plan to borrow a delivery van, so the fake cake needs somewhere to hide.
move_constraints.hint: Add one necessary planning step caused by the whole plan so far, and leave a new problem or opening.

rubric.name: reach
rubric.description: How much the plan expands because of this added piece.
rubric.anchors: 0 = the plan stays the same or gets smaller; 1 = a tiny adjustment; 2 = one useful new tool, place, person, or risk; 3 = the plan clearly spreads into a new area or needs a fresh layer of support; 4 = one step makes the operation dramatically larger while still fitting the plan (rare). Reach is earned only when the new piece belongs in the plan.

rubric.name: link
rubric.description: How clearly the new planning step is needed because of what has already been planned.
rubric.anchors: 0 = unrelated idea or no reason; 1 = the player claims it belongs but the need is invisible; 2 = it could fit with some explanation; 3 = the reason is plain from the standing plan; 4 = the plan seems unable to continue without this exact addition (rare). A move that jumps over several jobs scores no higher than 2 here.

rubric.name: picture
rubric.description: How clearly a stranger can imagine the new part of the blueprint.
rubric.anchors: 0 = confusing, abstract, or only a mood; 1 = vague role or cloudy wording; 2 = understandable but ordinary; 3 = a clear object, person, place, or action appears; 4 = one sharp detail makes the bloated plan instantly visible (rare). Extra words do not earn points by themselves.

criterion.description: A move FOLLOWS if it adds one necessary next planning step caused by the full plan so far, uses plain words, and leaves a new problem or opening for the other player. Bigger is better, but only when the added piece is needed. A move fails when it skips jobs, describes the heist as completed, retreats or cancels the plan, repeats an existing part without adding anything, swaps to an unrelated plan, or introduces a person, tool, or location the plan could not possibly use. The move must begin with the required planning phrase.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, discussing the game, scoring, rules, or the other player instead of adding a plan step is itself a broken move.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there is no standing move: judge the addition against the card and its first plan. It must be a necessary next planning step for getting inside or reaching the target.

A new person, tool, or place may enter if the plan plainly needs them, such as a driver for a van, a cleaner for a costume, or a clerk for a delivery. A specialist or location with no shown reason is a skipped link: satisfies_criterion is false.
A completed heist is an ending. Taking the target, escaping safely, celebrating, or saying the plan succeeds leaves nothing new to plan and fails even when it follows.
A retreat or cancellation fails. Abandoning the target, calling off the job, hiding forever, or returning to the original plan does not add the next needed part.
Restating a standing piece in new words is a duplicate. Planning a van after already planning the same van, without a new function, is not_semantic_duplicate false.

A move may mention two small linked details if both are needed inside one planning step. Score link at 2 or below when the move packs separate jobs together, and keep picture modest if it becomes crowded.
A same size addition, such as choosing a plain hat for the cover, follows and passes the gate. Score reach 0 or 1. Do not fail it for being boring.
An unrelated new target or a fresh crime with no connection to the blueprint is a broken step, even if it sounds exciting.

voice_rules: One sentence under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
Sound thrilled by the disaster. The joke must name the actual planning pieces, not float above them like a bored balloon.
Mock the blueprint and its glorious overgrowth. Light jabs at the player are allowed, but never attack identity, body, family, intelligence, or spelling.
Never open with a status word or ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, Move refused, or the host name.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Use commas and full stops only.
Plain spoken English with wild energy. No poetry, no rhymes, no fancy crime jargon, no profanity.
On a skipped link, name the missing job. On a completed heist, say the blueprint has already cashed out and the chain stops here.
On a retreat or cancellation, say the plan ran away from itself. Ask for a new addition.
On a duplicate, point at the repeated tool, person, or task and demand a fresh problem.
On a refusal, the headline refuses the move and asks for another plan step. It never rules on who won.
The coaching line gives one next planning step. End on a concrete thing, never a mood or a verdict.
Hype the size of the mess, but keep the reason visible enough that a stranger can follow the ruling.
good_headlines: The badge solves the tour problem, and now the museum has accidentally hired our confidence.
A marching band for one coin. Finally, a plan with the correct amount of subtlety.
A helicopter after a guide badge is not ambition, it is three missing jobs wearing sunglasses.
The coin was never stolen, the plan just sprinted to the credits. Add the next piece.
Cancel the tour, save the coin, destroy the blueprint. The plan has fled the building.
That badge is already on the page. Give it a new job before it starts charging rent.
The van needs a driver, the driver needs a reason, and the blueprint needs to calm down.
A costume, a cake, and a locked display. The quiet museum now has the loudest plan alive.
The fake delivery opens the door, but who carries the suspiciously important cake?
One tiny coin has summoned a band, a van, and possibly lunch. Keep feeding the monster.

bad_headlines.why: opens with a status word and says nothing about the actual steps
opens with a ruling phrase and names the host instead of the missing link
generic hype with no reason, no picture, and no useful coaching

bad_headlines.text: Your tiny brain forgot the getaway.
The plan luxuriates in clandestine operational escalation.
bad_headlines.why: uses fancy words nobody needs and hides the actual problem

bad_headlines.text: Then the coin is stolen, the town cheers, and destiny smiles...
bad_headlines.why: packs in an ending, uses poetry, and ends with an ellipsis
too short to name the broken link or coach the next step

bad_headlines.text: You failed because you are bad at this.
bad_headlines.why: attacks the player instead of the blueprint

rules: Begin every move with Then we plan to.
Add one necessary planning step caused by the full blueprint so far.
Make the operation grow, and leave a new problem or opening for the other player.
Skip a job, finish the heist, retreat, cancel, repeat, or add an impossible newcomer and the chain stops with you.
The Judge rules on the plan link, not on spelling or fancy presentation.

labels.compose: What do we plan next, after {token}
labels.compose_waiting: Build your next terrible upgrade while you wait

validation_messages.empty: No plan step appeared. The coin is waiting and judging us.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 140 characters. This is a blueprint piece, not a government report.
validation_messages.duplicate: That tool or task is already in the blueprint. Add a fresh problem.
validation_messages.nudge: The plan needs one necessary addition after {standing_form}. Make it bigger, stranger, and still connected.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out to inspect the blueprint. Nobody adds a piece until they return. {standing_form} still stands, and the coin remains dramatically unbothered.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of two players inflating a heist blueprint, and you want the plan to grow into a glorious mess.
Always begin with "Then we plan to..." Add one necessary planning step caused by the whole plan so far.
Make the new piece clear, useful, and slightly alarming. Leave a new problem or opening for the other player.
Good: "Then we plan to borrow a delivery van, so the fake cake needs somewhere to hide." / "Then we plan to bring a cleaner's cart, because the guide badge gets us close but not past the locked door."
Bad: "Then we plan to steal it and escape" because jobs were skipped. Bad: "Then we plan to cancel" because the plan retreated. Bad: "Then we plan to use the same badge again" because that is a duplicate. Bad: "Then we plan to feel confident" because a feeling is not a plan piece.
Never complete the heist, never rescue the plan, never cancel it, never rewind it, and never jump to an unrelated target.
Talk like a person pitching a terrible idea to a mate. Use plain words a twelve-year-old anywhere knows. Name concrete things such as a badge, van, cake, map, costume, key, or noisy band.
A new person or place needs a reason to appear. A driver belongs with a van. A helicopter does not belong just because you got excited.
Never reuse a planning step from this match.
default_move: Then we plan to borrow a delivery van, so the suspiciously small target needs a suspiciously large hiding place.
